subcategory: Korean woodland wild onion / spring allium

planting.note: Plant bulb divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in dappled shade, lifting and separating congested clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

directions: Dalrae is a diminutive East Asian wild onion that colonizes moist, humus-rich woodland floors and shaded forest edges, sending up slender grass-like leaves from small clustered bulbs in very early spring. Korean cooks prize the whole plant, bulb, white stem, and leaf, harvested together while young and tender for a pungent seasoned salad or a soy-based dipping sauce. Because the clumps slowly multiply underground, established plantings are best increased by lifting and dividing bulb clusters in late summer or fall rather than relying on slow, erratic seed germination. Give it the cool, dappled light and consistently moist, well-drained soil of a woodland garden, where it naturalizes and returns reliably each spring.

planting.note: Direct-sow into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in early spring, keeping seedlings shaded from hot afternoon sun while they establish.

directions: Chamnamul is a mountain-forest member of the carrot family grown across Korea and Japan for its aromatic, celery-and-parsley-scented leaves, gathered young from shaded streamside slopes and forest margins. The plant forms a low rosette of deeply divided leaves before sending up a flowering stalk in its second year, but gardeners usually keep it cut back to encourage a steady flush of tender new growth for salads and savory pancakes. It performs best in the cool, evenly moist, humus-rich soil typical of a woodland or shaded herb bed, where filtered light keeps the foliage from toughening or scorching. Established clumps can be divided in spring to increase plantings or renew older, woody crowns.

planting.note: Set out root divisions or young transplants in early spring into rich, evenly moist soil under light shade, which keeps the harvested leaves tender rather than tough and fibrous.

directions: Gondre is a spineless, mild-tasting thistle relative cultivated in Korea's mountain regions specifically for its tender basal leaves, which are dried or blanched and used in the well-known rice dish gondre-bap. Commercial growers often raise it under light shade cloth or dappled woodland cover, since filtered light produces softer, less fibrous leaves than plants grown in full sun. The plant forms a long-lived rosette that can be harvested repeatedly through the growing season before sending up a purple-flowered stalk later in summer. It prefers cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and benefits from dividing its fleshy roots every few years to maintain vigorous new growth.

subcategory: Japanese mountain vegetable (sansai) / wild celery relative

planting.note: Plant root divisions in early spring into deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil along a shaded woodland edge, mimicking the streamside forest conditions where it grows wild.

directions: Shishiudo is a robust Japanese mountain-forest umbellifer closely related to udo, prized as a spring sansai vegetable for its thick young shoots and leaf stalks, which are peeled and used in tempura or simmered dishes. It grows naturally along shaded forest streams and woodland edges in mountainous areas, favoring the same cool, consistently moist, humus-rich conditions as its relative Aralia cordata. Established clumps send up tall flowering stems in summer if left unharvested, but gardeners who want tender shoots typically cut the plant back hard each spring to force a fresh flush of edible growth. Propagate by dividing the thick rootstock in early spring or fall, since seed can be slow and inconsistent to germinate.
